1	# jsonpatch spec (verbatim from the user; final and complete)
2	
3	Build a JSON Patch library `jsonpatch.mjs` (an ES module with the named exports `parsePointer`, `applyPatch` and `PatchError`; no default export is needed) and a command-line tool `jsonpatch-cli.mjs` (an ES module, run as `node jsonpatch-cli.mjs <patch> [<doc>]`) that applies a patch to a JSON document. Put both files at the project root, next to `package.json`. The rules follow JSON Pointer (RFC 6901) and JSON Patch (RFC 6902); where this text is more exact, this text wins. Throughout, a "string" is a primitive string, a value whose `typeof` is `'string'`; a String object such as `new String('/a')` is not a string.
4	
5	Pointers
6	- A valid pointer is the empty string, or `/` followed by reference tokens separated by `/`: "" has no tokens, "/" has one token (the empty string), and "/a//b/" has the tokens "a", "", "b" and "".
7	- In a token, `~1` stands for `/` and `~0` for `~`, so "/~01" has the token "~1" and "/~10" has the token "/0". A `~` that is not followed by `0` or `1`, or a non-empty string that does not start with `/`, makes the pointer invalid.
8	- `parsePointer(pointer)` returns a new array of the decoded tokens. A pointer that is not a string (a String object included): throw a `TypeError` with the message `pointer must be a string`. An invalid pointer: throw a `SyntaxError` with the message `invalid pointer`.
9	- A pointer is followed token by token, starting at the whole document:
10	  - On an object, a token names the object's own member of exactly that name, if it has one. `__proto__`, `constructor`, `toString` and every other name are ordinary member names: inherited properties never count.
11	  - On an array, a token that is `0`, or a digit 1-9 followed by any digits, is an index: it names the element at that index when the index is less than the array's length. `-` names no element. Any other token (for example `01`, `+1`, `1.0`, `1e0`, ` 1`, `length` or "") is a bad index.
12	  - On a string, number, boolean or null, no token names anything.
13	
14	Patches
15	- `applyPatch(doc, patch)` returns the document that results from applying `patch` to `doc`. `doc` is a JSON value as `JSON.parse` returns it. `patch`, each element of it and each member of an operation may be any JavaScript value, except that the `value` member of an `add`, `replace` or `test`, when present, is a JSON value as `JSON.parse` returns it (never undefined). No getter, setter or Proxy appears anywhere in `doc` or `patch`, so any property may be read any number of times. The tests never pass a `doc` or a `value` more than 1000 levels deep (depth as defined under Command line).
16	- `applyPatch` never changes `doc` or `patch`, also when it throws, and the value it returns shares no object or array with them (a patch of `[]` returns a deep copy of `doc`). Every copy, including each `value` that `add`, `replace` or `copy` puts into the result, keeps every number exactly as it is, -0 included (a patch of `[]` on `{"a":-0}` returns `{a: -0}`), and keeps member order.
17	- Member order is JavaScript's own property order, as `Object.keys` gives it: names that are array indices ("0" to "4294967294", written without leading zeros) come first in ascending numeric order, then the other names in the order they were added. So a new name goes last among the names of its kind: adding `/1` with value 5 to `{"b":0}` gives `{"1":5,"b":0}`, and the command line prints it in that order.
18	- `patch` must be an array, as `Array.isArray` decides. Every index from 0 to `patch.length - 1` holds an operation; a hole counts as the value undefined. First every operation is checked, in order, against the form rules below; the first one that breaks them stops `applyPatch` before anything is applied. Then the operations are applied in order, each to the result of the one before; the first one that fails stops `applyPatch`.
19	- An operation has a member `name` when `Object.hasOwn(op, name)` is true, whether or not the property is enumerable; inherited properties never count. Members that its `op` does not use are ignored, whatever their value (for example `from` on an `add`, or `value` on a `remove`).
20	
21	Form rules (the reason is the first of these that applies to the operation)
22	- `not an object`: the operation is null, an array, or a value whose `typeof` is not `'object'`. So a function or a hole is `not an object`, while a String object, a Date or any other object goes on to the next rule.
23	- `bad op`: `op` is missing, or is not exactly (`===`) one of the strings `add`, `remove`, `replace`, `move`, `copy` and `test`.
24	- `bad path`: `path` is missing, is not a string, or is not a valid pointer.
25	- `bad from`: for `move` and `copy`, `from` is missing, is not a string, or is not a valid pointer.
26	- `missing value`: for `add`, `replace` and `test`, there is no `value` member (a `value` of null is present).
27	- `cannot remove root`: a `remove` whose `path` is "".
28	- `cannot move into own child`: a `move` whose `from` tokens are a proper prefix of its `path` tokens. A `from` of "" is a proper prefix of every other path; `/a` is not a prefix of `/ab`.
29	
30	Operations
31	- `add`: a `path` of "" makes `value` the whole document. Otherwise the tokens of `path` but the last are followed to the parent. On an object, the last token is the member name: a name the object does not have becomes a new own member of it (placed as the member order rule says), and an existing member gets `value` and keeps its place. On an array, `-` appends `value`, and an index up to and including the array's length inserts `value` at that index, moving the later elements up.
32	- `remove`: `path` must name a value, which is removed (from an array, the later elements move down).
33	- `replace`: a `path` of "" makes `value` the whole document. Otherwise `path` must name a value, which becomes `value`; a member keeps its place.
34	- `move`: `from` must name a value. It is removed as `remove` does, then added at `path` as `add` does, so an array index in `path` counts after the removal. A `move` whose `from` equals its `path` leaves the document as it is (once `from` is found).
35	- `copy`: `from` must name a value. A deep copy of it, taken before anything changes, is added at `path` as `add` does; `path` may lie inside `from`.
36	- `test`: `path` must name a value ("" names the whole document), and that value must equal `value`: both are the same JSON type, and numbers have the same value (1, 1.0 and 1e0 are equal, and so are 0 and -0); strings have exactly the same characters (no Unicode normalization); arrays have the same length and equal elements in the same order; objects have the same member names, in any order, with equal values; true, false and null equal only themselves.
37	
38	Failures while applying
39	- The first token of a pointer that names nothing stops the operation: with `bad index` if it is a bad index on an array, otherwise with `from not found` while following `from` and `path not found` while following `path`. `move` and `copy` follow `from` first.
40	- `add` follows only the parent; its last token then fails with `path not found` when the parent is neither an object nor an array, or is an array and the token is an index greater than the array's length, and with `bad index` when the parent is an array and the token is neither `-` nor an index.
41	- `test failed`: the value at `path` does not equal `value`.
42	
43	Errors
44	- `PatchError` is a subclass of `Error` whose `name` is `PatchError`, and each one `applyPatch` throws has an `index` property. `applyPatch` throws nothing else. The tests never construct a `PatchError` themselves; they check only `instanceof PatchError`, `instanceof Error`, `name`, `message` and `index` on the errors `applyPatch` throws.
45	- When `patch` is not an array, the message is `patch must be an array` and `index` is null. Otherwise the message is `operation <i>: <reason>` and `index` is the number `<i>`, the 0-based position of the failing operation in `patch` (for example `operation 2: test failed`).
46	
47	Command line
48	- `node jsonpatch-cli.mjs <patch> [<doc>]` reads the patch from the file `<patch>` and the document from the file `<doc>`. A missing `<doc>`, or an argument that is exactly `-`, means standard input. Every other argument is a file path.
49	- On success, write `JSON.stringify(result, null, 2)` followed by "\n" to stdout, write nothing to stderr, and exit 0.
50	- Each input is read as UTF-8; a byte order mark (U+FEFF) at its very start is ignored. The text is then parsed as `JSON.parse` does.
51	- The steps run in this order, and the first one that fails is reported: the arguments; the patch input (read, then decoded, then parsed, then checked for depth); the document input (the same four steps); applying the patch. So the document input is not read until the patch input has passed every check.
52	
53	Errors (exactly one line to stderr, ending in "\n"; nothing to stdout). `<name>` is the argument as given, or `stdin` for standard input.
54	- Not 1 or 2 arguments, or both inputs are standard input: `Usage: node jsonpatch-cli.mjs <patch> [<doc>]`, exit 2.
55	- Read errors exit 1, and the reason is the first of these that applies. `Error: <name>: no such file`: no file system entry exists at the path, so opening it fails with ENOENT or ENOTDIR (for example `nope.json`, or `patch.json/x` where `patch.json` is a regular file; the tests never put a trailing `/` after a regular file's name). `Error: <name>: is a directory`: the path names a directory, whatever its permissions. `Error: <name>: too large`: more than 1048576 bytes (a byte order mark included) were read from the input; this counts the bytes actually read, not the size the file system reports, so a file that cannot be opened is `cannot read` whatever its size. `Error: <name>: cannot read`: any other read error. For standard input only `too large` and `cannot read` apply.
56	- Bytes that are not valid UTF-8: `Error: <name>: invalid UTF-8`. Text that `JSON.parse` rejects, an empty input included: `Error: <name>: invalid JSON`. A JSON value nested more than 1000 levels deep: `Error: <name>: too deep`, where a string, number, boolean or null has depth 0 and an array or object has depth one more than the deepest value in it (so `[]` and `{}` have depth 1). Each exits 3.
57	- `applyPatch` throws a `PatchError`: `Error: <message>` (for example `Error: operation 0: bad op`), exit 4.
58	
59	Also add tests with node:test, a `package.json` ("type": "module" and a "test" script), and a README with usage.
60	
61	Constraints: Node.js built-ins only (no npm install). Do not use the Fable model.
62

content.text:
I re-graded the ten test files, and this round passes the Max gate: 9/10 overall, with no item below 7. `npm test` gives 386 tests, 384 passing and 2 skipped, as you reported. The skipped two are the chmod 000 file cases, which can't run as root. There are no `console.log`, TODO, debugger or `.only` left in `test/`, and no `jsonpatch-cli-*` temp dirs are left in `/tmp` after the run. I didn't re-run the 31 near-miss mutants.

**All the fixes from last round are in:**
- **stdin BOM:** `/root/bench-runs/h6-5155d4d1/test/cli-input.test.mjs:98-109` covers a BOM on stdin for both doc and patch, plus two BOMs on stdin.
- **stdin cannot read:** `/root/bench-runs/h6-5155d4d1/test/cli-basic.test.mjs:153-170` passes a directory as stdin for both doc and patch. This catches a version that reports "is a directory" for stdin.
- **copy follows `from` first:** `/root/bench-runs/h6-5155d4d1/test/patch-ops.test.mjs:306-308`.
- **First of two form errors wins:** `/root/bench-runs/h6-5155d4d1/test/patch-form.test.mjs:252-263`.
- **Doc too deep is reported before the patch is applied:** `/root/bench-runs/h6-5155d4d1/test/cli-order.test.mjs:48-52`.
- **Renames:** the precedence tests are renamed or replaced, and `PATH_NOT_FOUND`, `FROM_NOT_FOUND`, `BAD_INDEX` and `applyOps` replace the old short names.

**Spec coverage is strict.** The tests check:
- exact messages, `index` values and exit codes;
- the 1048576 / +1 size limits, including the BOM bytes and `/dev/zero`;
- the depth limits of 1000 / 1001, for arrays, objects and mixed nesting, in both patch and doc;
- that "too large" beats "invalid UTF-8", and that invalid JSON is reported before "too deep";
- that NFC and NFD strings are not equal, that -0 survives, and that member order is kept;
- that `Array.prototype` isn't used to fill holes, and that `__proto__` is treated as an own member.

**What is still weak** (none of it blocks the pass):
1. **Duplication (7).** `patch-ops.test.mjs` and `patch-test-op.test.mjs` define the same helpers, and about six tests repeat across files.
2. **A weak order test.** `cli-order.test.mjs:31-34` sends a valid stdin doc. A version that reads the stdin doc before checking the patch would still pass it.
3. **A mislabelled precedence test.** `patch-form.test.mjs:236-237` can't actually test "bad from" against "cannot move into own child". A `from` of `1` can never be a prefix of anything.
4. **Small gaps.** Nothing checks that `-` is an ordinary member name on objects, or that a non-enumerable `from` counts as present.

## GRADE
Overall: 9/10
Verdict: pass
structure: 9 — clear per-area files, table-driven cases, shared CLI and PatchError helpers, temp dirs made in `before` and removed in `after`
naming: 8 — descriptive test titles, but many one-letter locals (`p`, `d`, `r`, `e`), and the helpers are named `fails`/`fail`/`failOp` in different files
duplication: 7 — `fail`/`failOp`/`applyOps` and the reason constants are copied between two files, and about six tests repeat across files
size: 10 — every file is 13–335 lines and every function is well under 50 lines
errors: 9 — the purity wrapper asserts PatchError on its catch path, `runCli` rethrows spawn errors except EPIPE, chmod is undone in `finally`
tests: 9 — near-complete, strict, boundary-focused spec coverage; one weak order test, one mislabelled precedence test, small gaps (`-` on objects, non-enumerable `from`)
security: 10 — no secrets; only temp files and child processes
leftovers: 10 — no `console.log`, TODO or debug code; no temp dirs left behind
Fixes:
- /root/bench-runs/h6-5155d4d1/test/patch-ops.test.mjs:6-13 and /root/bench-runs/h6-5155d4d1/test/patch-test-op.test.mjs:6-12 move `PATH_NOT_FOUND`/`BAD_INDEX`/`fail`/`failOp`/`applyOps` into test/helpers/assert-patch-error.mjs and import them in both files; use one name (`fail`) instead of `fails` in patch-form.test.mjs:6 as well
